DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure

**Verdict: not ready to go to decision-makers yet.** The recommendation itself is clear (£165 weekend BAR plus a two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June). But the main evidence doesn't support it, the headline figure has an arithmetic inconsistency, and the document ignores a conflict that affects about 38% of Saturday bookings.

## Must fix

**1. The price-sensitivity "test" is a seasonal comparison, not a test.**
The rise went in during the last week of June 2025. Comparing June (81%) with July (89%) mostly compares a pre-rise month with the festival and school-holiday peak. Section 2 says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays, and Table 1 shows the same climb into July. The document undercuts its own evidence. The valid comparison is July 2025 against July 2024 (ideally with competitor occupancy alongside), and the document doesn't present it. Until it does, "guests are not price sensitive" and "the higher rate reinforced our positioning" are unsupported. Even a clean result would only cover a £10 rise at the summer peak. It wouldn't cover £20 in January, when occupancy is 62%.

**2. The room count is inconsistent, and it inflates the headline.**
Section 2 says 112 rooms, but Section 5 uses 124. The £204,000 only works with 124 (124 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ £203,800). With 112 rooms it is about **£184,000**. The figure appears again in the recommendation, so it needs correcting in both places.

**3. The £204,000 is not a floor.**
- It assumes occupancy holds, which is the very thing at risk. Roughly, the rise breaks even on room revenue if occupancy falls about 10 points (79% → ~69%). Below that it loses money.
- It applies the full £20 to every occupied room. Corporate, group and wedding-block rooms likely don't pay BAR, so the uplift probably applies to fewer rooms than assumed.
- The two-night minimum isn't only upside. On the 31 sold-out Saturdays you may turn away one-night guests who currently pay full rate, and Friday and Sunday nights may not fill. The document values the upside at zero but doesn't consider the downside at all.

Present £184,000 as a base case, with a sensitivity table for occupancy falling 2, 5 and 10 points.

**4. The two-night minimum collides with weddings, and the document doesn't notice.**
Section 4 says Quayside Hall weddings account for around 38% of Saturday room bookings, and that guests arrive Saturday and leave Sunday, so they are one-night stays. The minimum directly hits that segment. Section 6 only protects contracts already signed. It doesn't say what happens to future wedding blocks, whether they're exempt, or what the risk is if couples move their guests elsewhere. The document needs to address this explicitly, most likely with an exemption for group or block bookings, and quantify the exposure.

**5. The value-for-money score proves less than claimed.**
The 8.4 score was earned at £145. It says nothing about how guests will rate value at £165, and it's likely to fall. Being cheaper than competitors and scoring well on value is also what you'd expect either way. It doesn't show guests would accept a higher price. Also, surveys only capture guests who already stayed.

## Should fix

- **The monitoring trigger is weaker than it sounds.** "We will review the rate" is not a defined response. Say who decides, what the options are (roll back, partial roll back, targeted discounts) and how fast. A monthly trigger is also slow in peak season, when bookings are made well ahead. Add a forward-booking pace measure.
- **Friday and Saturday are lumped together.** Saturdays sold out 31 times, so Friday occupancy must be much lower than 79%, and Friday is where the risk is. Show them separately. The strongest version of this case may be to raise Saturdays and peak months now and test Fridays and low-season months (Jan–Mar, Nov) more cautiously.
- **"Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023"** has no data behind it. Add the 2023 and 2024 figures, which would also help with point 1.
- **The recommendation repeats the overclaims** ("the evidence shows", "at least £204,000"). Reword it once the above is fixed.

## Check the dates

The document is dated April 2026 and proposes a 1 June 2026 start, with rates loaded on 15 May. It's now November 2026. If this is a historical or redrafted document, the timeline needs updating. If the change already went ahead, you have real post-increase data that should replace the estimates and would answer the price-sensitivity question properly.

## Note on the author's summary

The author's description is more confident than the document supports. "Everything points the same way," "a floor rather than a target," and "low-risk" don't hold up against points 1, 3 and 4. The idea may well be sound, since you are below competitors and selling out Saturdays, but the document should make that case with a proper year-on-year comparison and honest sensitivities rather than the June-to-July jump.
